title: Bally/Chaussures de Travail
description: An unusal kind of advertising image: With its powerful figures of peasants striding across the fields (echoes of Van Gogh and Millet!), and the woman's red kerchief, this could be a Socialist Realist paean to farm work rather than an ad for work shoes. Skirt and man's shirt are blue, vest and pants khaki, soil red-brown. Cardnaux designed several posters for Bally between 1924 and '26. This was one of his last commercial designs. Rare! Literature: Cardinaux, 128; PAI-XV, 178. Variant

title: Bally
description: Villemot manages to make the two female torsos look like a giant lotus blossom. The only color in the poster is on the shoes, guaranteeing that the product is the focus of our attention. His study for this poster was, in fact, titled “Lotus” and on publication was quickly dubbed “Les Femmes-Fleurs”–as it has been the the practice to give such titles to each of his Bally images. title: Bally
description: A year after Cappiello created this slick poster for Bally, a contemporary critic used it as an example of the artist’s mastery in giving utilitarian objects special treatment: “Even for Bally, where two different shoes are pictured, Cappiello can’t limit himself to a strict interpretation. His subtle imagination doesn’t give us the shoes on feet; with unequaled elegance, he places the man’s oxford on a silken palm and holds the narrow heel of the woman’s pump in his fingers as if it were a work of art” (Pierre Guéguin, in Cappiello, pp. 154-5). This is the largest, 3-sheet format. Literature: Ref: Cappiello/Rennert, 515 (var); Cappiello, 341; PAI-XL, 274C

title: Bally
description: For thirty years, Villemot was one of the finest French posterists, unsurpassed at setting the right mood with just a few simple lines and bold colors. This represents the very first poster which he executed for Bally shoes, one of his longest-standing clients. Villemot spoke of the advertisement fondly: “The poster appeared on the walls at the beginning of September. These two legs attracted the eye with the power of the graphics, seducing it with the draftsmanship and color . . . The poster isn’t only capable of selling the product at a precise moment . . . Moreover, I arrived at this conclusion: The poster needs to be known by the non-buyers. Take shoes for example . . . This poster is going to be seen by passer-bys that have no need to replace their shoes, who don’t have money for that . . . The message of the poster needs to confirm the make’s image, one day transforming the non-buyer into a client for this brand. Jean-Pierre Rocher [Head of Publicity at Bally] understood that very well. He wanted to create a ‘Bally image,’ memorized [by the public] as we now say” (Villemot, p. 86). A very successful design, described by Vendre of October, 1967, as “a high-class work.” Literature: Ref: Schweizer Plakate, 368; Villemot, p. 87 (var); Villemot A-Z, p. 115 (var); Villemot/La Femme, p. 65; PAI-XXVII, 611

title: Bally
description: In this poster for Bally flats and heels, Villemont uses hues that glow with profound intensity and a seated model that appears to be little more than a disassemble mannequin to forcibly grab our attention and focus it on the brand-name. The irrepressible artist could always be counted on to come up with something fresh, carefully calculated to create a riveting impression. Literature: Ref: Villemot A-Z, p. 114; Villemot/La Femme, p. 69 (var); PAI-IX, 533b

Founded in 1851 in Switzerland, Bally continues to produce luxury leather shoes to this day.

title: Bally : Maquette
description: Villemot’s preparatory work for his 1974 poster shows a fairly seamless transition from conception to final product, with many of the compositional elements remaining in tact. The duo were inspired by Villemot’s wife, who he had previously represented in a similar coiled up position. Villemot called this work “Lotus,” and in the finalized version, the negative space between the women’s backs takes on a more floral resemblance. The poster was later called “Les Femmes-Fleurs,” in keeping with the practice of titling Villemot’s Bally images. Literature: Ref (all var): Bon Salle, 306; Villemot/Forney, 120; PAI-XLI, 581

description: Posters for Bally shoes always put style first, and these two complimentary designs have a flair that lands them among the best of the bunch. Gid was a respected graphic artist who originally studied architecture but later went into commercial design, illustration, and typography; in posters, he favored the cinema, producing a number of works for major French directors. (2) Literature: Ref: PAI-XIV, 267

title: Bally
description: It shouldn't work, but it does: this tripping, off-kilter jumble of reds, blacks, blues, browns, and the palest pink amid Villemot's tangle of legs and shoes manages to be witty, flirtatious, and a little erotic at the same time. This is the larger version of the poster. Literature: Ref: Bon Salle, 307; Villemot/La Femme, p. 68; Villemot/A to Z, p. 27; Villemot/Forney, 121; PAI-LXXXIV, 493

title: Bally
description: For the Swiss shoe manufacturer Bally, Barberis conjures not only a stylish advertising poster, but a smart shoe box as well.

title: Bally Lyon / "Le Meilleur Marché Par La Qualité"
description: This particularly rare Cappiello deploys a similar idea to the artist's Mossant posters—a celebratory lifting-to-the-air of the treasured item—this time for Bally shoes. Note the theatrical, cinematic lighting, which is possibly a nod to Charlie Chaplin, who was also commissioned by Bally for commercial work during this time period. Literature: Cappiello/Rennert, 515 (var); PAI-LXXIII, 233

title: Bally vintage poster
description: Villemot created many posters and advertising images for Bally, all of which are bold, charming, and winsomely designed. Here, our leggy model bounces the world off of her Bally pump, while her shadow gives a hint of the store's men's offerings. Literature: Bon Salle, 313; Villemot/La Femme, cover & p. 32; Villemot/A to Z, p. 116; Affiches 1000, 0731; Encyclopédie/Weill, p. 113; Publicité, p. 208; PAI-LXXVIII, 481
